title: Lay aside all earthly cares
hook: in the Cherubic hymn of the Liturgy, the people join the angels

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mount Athos: monks on a cliff, praying for the world. Your line was the holy mountain. Which stranger got your prayer or your good wish? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-six.

Partway through the Orthodox Divine Liturgy, the singing slows right down. The choir begins a hymn so drawn out that a single word can take a long breath to sing. A door in the screen of icons opens. The clergy come out carrying the bread and wine for communion, and walk them through the church with candles and incense, then back through the central doors to the altar. And the words the choir is singing ask everyone standing there to do something hard. Put it all down. Not later. Now. Today's word is the hymn's own phrase: lay aside all earthly cares.

It's called the Cherubic Hymn. In substance it says: we who, in a mystery, represent the cherubim, and sing the thrice-holy hymn to the life-giving Trinity, let us now lay aside all earthly cares, so that we may receive the King of all, escorted unseen by the hosts of angels. Alleluia. Look at what that claims. The people in the room, tired, distracted, holding coats and children, stand for the cherubim, angels the Bible places close to God. And the thrice-holy hymn is the song Isaiah heard the seraphim crying to one another in his vision: "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory." To receive the King of all, the hymn says, everything else gets set down. The Greek word for care in the hymn is merimna: worry, the pull of a divided mind. The Bible knows that pull. In the Sermon on the Mount Jesus says, "Take therefore no thought for the morrow." And Peter's first letter says, "Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you." Notice what none of these says. None says your cares don't matter. Peter says where to throw them. The hymn says to lay them aside, for now, like a bag set down at a door, so you can be fully in the room. They'll still be there when the service ends. But for a few minutes, they won't be running it.
screen: `A BAG SET DOWN AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: set down one care before praying. Sit, and rest your hands open on your knees. Name the care that's heaviest right now. Just one. Feel its weight for a breath, as if it were in your hands. Then slowly set it down beside you, the way you'd put a bag on the floor by a door. It isn't gone. You can pick it up after. If you pray, you can hand it over with Peter's line: casting all your care upon him. If you don't, simply sit with empty hands. The bell holds the time.
Lay aside all earthly cares. The line from the Cherubic Hymn that asks the people to set their worries down and sing with the angels.
screen: `LAY ASIDE ALL EARTHLY CARES — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: lay aside all cares. Before one thing today, a meal, a meeting, a conversation, set your worries down at the door, phone included, and pick them up after. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: In the Orthodox Divine Liturgy the choir sings the Cherubic Hymn while the clergy carry the bread and wine in procession, the Great Entrance; the people stand, and some cross themselves and bow as the gifts pass.

what a scholar hears: merimna, the divided mind; Jesus says take no thought for the morrow, and Peter says casting all your care upon him.

notes: The Cherubic Hymn is paraphrased ('in substance'), not quoted; English renderings vary. Confirm the paraphrase.
Greek: πᾶσαν τὴν νῦν βιωτικὴν ἀποθώμεθα μέριμναν. Confirm μέριμνα; Matthew 6:34 uses μεριμνήσητε and 1 Peter 5:7 uses μέριμναν.
'cherubim, angels the Bible places close to God' (ark, Ezekiel); Isaiah 6 names seraphim, and the script says so. Confirm the phrasing.
Great Entrance described generally (clergy leave by a side door of the iconostasis and return by the central doors). Practices vary by place; confirm.
howItsDone: crossing and bowing as the gifts pass is described as what some do; confirm.

Editor pass: 'you'll need your hands free' was not in the hymn (now 'to receive the King of all, everything else gets set down'); cut the Greek word-family claims linking merimna to Matthew 6:34 and 1 Peter 5:7 from teach, original note and trapdoor under the claims rule; fixed the carry's grammar (worries ... them).
Audit: vague line 'Peter says to throw them somewhere' sharpened to 'Peter says where to throw them' (1 Peter 5:7, upon him).
